node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sampling distribution statistic definition
node.description: Identify the statistic whose repeated-sample variation is described by a sampling distribution.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Unbiased estimator check
node.description: Check whether a statistic is centred on the population parameter it is intended to estimate.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Standard error and sample size relationship
node.description: Explain how standard error usually decreases as sample size increases, holding population variability fixed.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Standard error units
node.description: Interpret the units of a standard error as the same units as the statistic or estimate being described.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Mean standard error formula
node.description: Use the standard error formula for a sample mean, usually standard deviation divided by the square root of sample size.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Proportion standard error formula
node.description: Use the standard error formula for a sample proportion from a binomial or large-sample normal approximation context.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Interval endpoint calculation
node.description: Calculate lower and upper confidence-interval endpoints from an estimate and margin of error.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Interval width interpretation
node.description: Interpret interval width as reflecting uncertainty in an estimate, not the spread of raw data values.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Parameter plausibility from interval
node.description: Use a confidence interval to judge which parameter values are plausible under the inference method and context.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Random condition check
node.description: Check whether data were collected with random sampling or random assignment appropriate to the inference question.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Independence ten percent check
node.description: Use the ten percent condition as a practical check for approximate independence when sampling without replacement.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Mean normality or CLT check
node.description: Check whether a mean-based inference procedure is justified by population normality, sample size or central-limit-theorem reasoning.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Proportion large-counts check
node.description: Check whether success and failure counts are large enough for a normal approximation in proportion inference.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Null hypothesis parameter statement
node.description: Write a null hypothesis as a claim about a population parameter rather than a sample statistic.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Alternative hypothesis direction choice
node.description: Choose a one-sided or two-sided alternative hypothesis that matches the research question before seeing results.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: One-sided tail area selection
node.description: Select the correct tail area for a one-sided hypothesis test based on the alternative hypothesis direction.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Two-sided p-value reasoning
node.description: Interpret a two-sided p-value as accounting for results at least as extreme in either direction from the null value.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Test statistic observed distance
node.description: Interpret a test statistic as the observed estimate's standardised distance from the null value.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Reject or fail-to-reject wording
node.description: Use reject or fail-to-reject language accurately when comparing p-values with a significance level.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Conclusion links parameter context and evidence
node.description: Write inference conclusions that name the population parameter, context, evidence strength and uncertainty.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Statistical versus practical significance
node.description: Distinguish statistical significance from practical importance or effect size in context.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sampling distribution describes statistic variation
node.description: A sampling distribution describes how a statistic varies across repeated samples, not how individual data values vary.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Standard error has statistic units
node.description: A standard error is measured in the same units as the estimate or statistic whose sampling variation it describes.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Interval endpoints use margin of error
node.description: Confidence interval endpoints are found by subtracting and adding the margin of error to the estimate.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Fail to reject does not prove null
node.description: Failing to reject a null hypothesis means insufficient evidence against it, not proof that it is true.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Standard error is sample standard deviation
node.description: Learner treats standard error as the spread of raw sample data rather than the sampling variation of an estimate.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Interval width is raw data spread
node.description: Learner interprets confidence interval width as the range or spread of individual observations rather than uncertainty in a parameter estimate.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Two-sided p-value uses one tail only
node.description: Learner reports only one tail area for a two-sided test instead of accounting for both directions of extremeness.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Reject null proves alternative
node.description: Learner treats rejecting the null hypothesis as proving the alternative hypothesis with certainty.

edge.rationale: Identifying the statistic is central to reasoning about a sampling distribution.
Interpreting units is part of understanding standard error as a statistic's sampling variation.
Endpoint calculation directly practises the estimate plus-or-minus margin structure.
Two-sided p-values are a core use case of p-value tail-area reasoning.
The statistic must be identified within the broader idea of a sampling distribution.
edge.failure_signal: Learner confuses a sampling distribution with the raw data distribution.

edge.rationale: Checking unbiasedness requires comparing the sampling distribution centre with the population parameter.
edge.failure_signal: Learner says an estimate is unbiased because one sample estimate is close to the parameter.

edge.rationale: Sample size effects are understood through sampling distribution spread.
edge.failure_signal: Learner thinks increasing sample size changes the raw-data spread in the same way as standard error.

edge.rationale: Unit interpretation follows from the meaning of standard error.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats standard error as unitless or as raw-data range.

edge.rationale: Formula use follows the concept of standard error for a mean.
edge.failure_signal: Learner divides by n rather than square root of n, or uses the wrong standard deviation.

edge.rationale: Formula use follows the concept of standard error for a sample proportion.
edge.failure_signal: Learner uses a mean standard-error formula for a proportion.

edge.rationale: Confidence interval endpoints require a margin of error.
edge.failure_signal: Learner adds only one endpoint or reverses lower and upper endpoints.

edge.rationale: Interpreting width depends on identifying endpoints and the uncertainty interval they form.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats interval width as the raw-data range.

edge.rationale: Plausibility claims rely on interpreting what confidence intervals mean.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats every value outside the interval as impossible rather than not supported by the interval method.

edge.rationale: Random sampling or random assignment is one of the core inference condition checks.
edge.failure_signal: Learner proceeds with inference without checking how data were collected.

edge.rationale: The ten percent check refines independence reasoning in sampling contexts.
edge.failure_signal: Learner assumes observations are independent even when the sample is a large fraction of the population.

edge.rationale: Mean inference conditions include normality or central-limit-theorem support.
edge.failure_signal: Learner uses a mean interval despite severe skew and small sample size without qualification.

edge.rationale: Proportion intervals require success-failure count checks for normal approximation support.
edge.failure_signal: Learner uses a normal approximation when expected success or failure counts are too small.

edge.rationale: Null hypotheses should be stated about a population parameter, not a sample statistic.
edge.failure_signal: Learner writes H0 using the observed sample statistic rather than a hypothesised parameter value.

edge.rationale: Alternative hypotheses are paired with the null parameter statement and research direction.
edge.failure_signal: Learner chooses a one-sided direction after seeing the data rather than from the question context.

edge.rationale: Tail selection depends on the alternative hypothesis direction.
edge.failure_signal: Learner calculates the upper tail for a lower-tail alternative, or vice versa.

edge.rationale: Two-sided p-value reasoning extends p-value-as-tail-area reasoning to both directions.
edge.failure_signal: Learner reports only one tail area for a two-sided test.

edge.rationale: A standardised test statistic represents observed distance from the null value.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats the test statistic as the raw estimate or as the p-value.

edge.rationale: Decision wording follows from comparing the p-value with alpha.
edge.failure_signal: Learner says accept the null or prove the alternative instead of using appropriate decision language.

edge.rationale: Contextual conclusions build on the formal decision while naming parameter, context and evidence.
edge.failure_signal: Learner gives a statistical decision without translating it back to context.

edge.rationale: Practical significance is judged after a statistical conclusion is linked to context and effect size.
edge.failure_signal: Learner assumes a small p-value automatically means an important real-world effect.
